findings.message: A different agent (Claude) checked the work in a separate headless process.

The Go package-context lint change is wired through real collaborators. post-tool-lint.ts calls lint.ts, then safewordCli, then the hidden `hook go-lint` command, then goLint, which uses prepareGoLintConfig and goLintProcess. The Codex hook reaches the same path through runPackagedHook, and SAFEWORD_PLUGIN_CLI points at dist/cli.js. Fakes appear only at the golangci-lint executable boundary, and a separate CI matrix (v2.0.0 with Go 1.24, v2.13.2 with Go 1.25) runs the real linter with SAFEWORD_REQUIRE_GO_LINT=1, so a missing tool fails rather than skips. Package loading is nonrecursive with cwd set to the edited file's directory and no --fix. The four relative-path modes are frozen to a cfg-mode temporary file in the original base, and config-path interpolation is limited to v2.1 and later. Report and resource paths become absolute against the original cwd. Malformed or old helper responses produce warnings and never a false clean result. Warnings are kept alongside errors, the payload is capped at 16 KiB with a truncation notice, and cleanup is covered on success, error and signal. I found no concrete path that reports clean lint while the accepted claim is false. The remaining concerns are missing proof for one promised input class and documented residual limits.

The design says to test YAML legacy-boolean inputs (yes/no/on/off) against the real linter and to warn when a construct cannot be represented faithfully. parseYamlConfig rejects only legacy octals. Legacy booleans are passed through as YAML 1.2 strings, and neither config.test.ts nor lint-go-context.test.ts covers that case. go-yaml with Viper's weak decoding could interpret these scalars differently from the frozen JSON, which may silently change one policy key. Add a characterization test or reject the case explicitly.

prepareGoLintConfig writes the temporary config into the original base, which can be outside the project root. Examples: the home-directory fallback config in cfg mode (writes into ~), an outer gitroot, or an outer go.mod in gomod mode. The design accepts this for the base, but nothing tells the user when the temporary file lands outside the Safeword project, and residue left after SIGKILL would then sit in an unrelated directory.

In goLint, signal handlers are registered in goLintProcess only after prepareGoLintConfig has already created the temporary file. A SIGTERM, SIGINT or SIGHUP in that window, while the version probe or path computation runs, leaves an untracked .safeword-go-lint-*.json behind. This is narrow and matches the documented best-effort limit, but registering the handlers before materializing the file would close it.

lint-config-fallback.test.ts asserts the Go invocations with expect.arrayContaining, so it does not check that fmt runs before run. It also only uses stubs; the subprocess-cwd assertions the design requires are covered only in lifecycle.test.ts (via $PWD in the trace). The ordering guarantee, format first and then lint once without --fix, relies on the real-linter test in lint-go-context.test.ts that keeps a fixable misspelling.

TOML parsing goes through smol-toml defaults. Dates are rejected by assertJson, which is correct. Integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER could lose precision without an error, depending on smol-toml's default integer handling. This is unlikely for golangci configs but is not covered by the 'reject lossy input' tests.

The new go-lint-context CI job is not in the `needs` list of the deploy jobs. That is consistent with how the cli-contract job is handled and does not affect the Go lint claim. Make it a required branch-protection check if it is meant to gate merges.
